confidence_note: This is the opening chapter of Outliers. Kept: the Medicine Hat Tigers' roster from the 2007 Memorial Cup, where most players were born early in the year; the Canadian youth hockey eligibility cutoff of January 1; the observation by psychologist Roger Barnsley in the mid-1980s, first noticed at a junior hockey game in Lethbridge; Gladwell's figure that in elite groups of hockey players about 40 percent are born January to March; and the 'Matthew Effect' of accumulative advantage. The Medicine Hat roster is described without precise percentages. The TR text's other figures are omitted where not needed.
facts: Gladwell opens Outliers with the Medicine Hat Tigers, a Canadian junior hockey team that played in the 2007 Memorial Cup final.
Looking at the roster, a striking number of players were born in January, February, March or April.
The pattern was first noticed by Canadian psychologist Roger Barnsley in the mid-1980s, when he was at a junior hockey game in Lethbridge and saw the players' birth dates in the program.
Barnsley found the same pattern across elite youth hockey: in any elite group of Canadian hockey players, about 40 percent are born between January and March.
The reason is the eligibility cutoff of January 1. A boy born in January plays against boys born as late as December, and at age nine or ten that gap in physical maturity is large.
Coaches pick the bigger, more coordinated boys for elite teams, where they get better coaching, more games and more practice. Over time they genuinely become better players.
Gladwell calls this accumulative advantage, or the 'Matthew Effect': small early differences grow into large ones.
tension: The best young hockey players in Canada share a surprising trait that has nothing to do with talent: their birth month.
opening_idea: Look at the birth dates on an elite hockey roster and a strange pattern jumps out.

lessons.idea: What looks like talent can be early maturity.
Small early advantages compound through selection.
Systems can be redesigned to reduce arbitrary advantage.

reflect: Where did you get an early head start you didn't earn?
Who might be judged 'less talented' now just because they're early in their development?
reflect_final: Whose potential are you judging too early?

use_cases.situation: Your team is choosing interns for a fast-track program after one assessment.
use_cases.move: Suggest a second evaluation later, so late developers aren't locked out.

use_cases.situation: Your younger-for-the-class child feels behind classmates.
use_cases.move: Explain that months matter at their age and focus on their own progress over time.

use_cases.situation: You wrote yourself off in a field after an early setback.
use_cases.move: Ask whether you were judged too early, and try again with fresh practice.

pocket_idea: An early head start can look exactly like talent.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Canada's top junior hockey players are unusually likely to be born in January.

conversation_variants.question_idea: Where did an early head start get mistaken for talent?
